title: Edmonton Warns Diwali Fireworks Without Permit Are Illegal, Fines Reach $10,000
excerpt: Only certified professionals with a city permit may launch fireworks in Edmonton. For Diwali, a free permitted display runs at Mill Woods Park on Sunday, November 8, with fireworks at 8:30 p.m.
body:
• Using fireworks without a permit is illegal anywhere inside Edmonton city limits, and only Natural Resources Canada-certified professionals with an Edmonton Fire Rescue Services permit may launch them.
  • Breaking the rules can bring fines of up to $10,000 and, depending on the circumstances, criminal charges that can lead to a criminal record and possible jail time.
  • For Diwali, the city is backing a free, permitted celebration at Mill Woods Park on Sunday, November 8, 2026, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., with fireworks at 8:30 p.m. — no home permit needed to attend.
  • Permits take up to 10 working days to process, so a last-minute home display is not an option: apply through Edmonton Fire Rescue Services or attend a permitted display instead.

With Diwali approaching, Edmonton is reminding residents that setting off fireworks at home without a permit is illegal — and that the penalty for ignoring the rule can reach $10,000. Edmonton Fire Rescue Services is urging families to leave fireworks to professionals and to use permitted displays during the celebrations, according to the city's fireworks guidance and reporting on the city's Diwali reminder.

Diwali in 2026 runs from Dhanteras on November 6 through Bhai Dooj on November 11 in The Videshi's published festival coverage, and fireworks are traditional for many families. In Edmonton, that tradition has to take a different form: a professionally run display, not a backyard launch.

What the rule actually says

The City of Edmonton states plainly that the unpermitted use of fireworks is prohibited within city limits. Only professionals who are certified by Natural Resources Canada and who hold an approved firework permit issued by Edmonton Fire Rescue Services are allowed to use fireworks in the city. Any use of fireworks requires proper permitting under the city's bylaws, and an approved permit is valid for one event only.

"Fireworks can cause serious injuries and fires when not handled by professionals, especially in a city with many wood-framed homes," said Graeme McAlister, Deputy Chief, Community Safety and Risk, at Edmonton Fire Rescue Services, in comments reported from the city's reminder. Permits, the city notes, are issued only to certified operators who have prepared safety plans specific to their display sites, including measures to control and suppress fires.

The free Diwali display at Mill Woods Park

Instead of home fireworks, the city is encouraging families to attend a professionally managed celebration: a free Diwali and Bandi Chhor Diwas event at Mill Woods Park on Sunday, November 8, 2026. The celebration begins at 5 p.m., with festivities running to 9 p.m. and the fireworks scheduled for 8:30 p.m. to 8:45 p.m., weather permitting. The programme includes cultural performances, speeches and food trucks.

The event is brought to the community by The Sifarish Network and Jhajj Productions, in partnership with community supporters and with support from the City of Edmonton, and no tickets are required. "Diwali is a celebration of light, joy and community," said Sunny Kakar, Executive Director and Co-Chair of The Sifarish Network, who also encouraged residents to consider their neighbours, pets and nearby homes when celebrating. Full details are on the United Edmonton Diwali and Bandi Chhor Diwas event listing.

How permits work — and why sparklers are different

For organisers who want their own display, applicants must email a completed checklist to Edmonton Fire Rescue Services, and processing can take up to 10 working days. The city's Firework Permits and Safety page lists the fees: $100 for a consumer firework permit, $181 for a display firework permit and $135 for a pyrotechnic device permit. A copy of the permit must be on site during use and shown to officials on request, and organisers are expected to work with a Fire Prevention Officer to pre-approve the site.

Handheld sparklers are treated differently. Families can still use sparklers during their celebrations, provided adults supervise their use. The city warns that sparklers burn at extremely high temperatures and should never be used near dry grass, wooden decks or loose clothing, and that used sparklers should be thoroughly soaked in water and allowed to cool before being placed in the garbage.

What happens if you ignore the rule

Using fireworks without a permit is a violation of Edmonton bylaws. The city says failure to comply with the codes, regulations, bylaws and permitting around fireworks is illegal and subject to enforcement, which can include fines of up to $10,000. Criminal charges can also be laid depending on the circumstances, which can result in a criminal record, further fines and the possibility of jail time.

Anyone who sees a fire or someone who needs help should call 911. Firework complaints go to 311, or to the Edmonton Police Service non-emergency line at 780-423-4567 (#377 from a mobile). The practical Diwali plan is simple: diyas, sweets and supervised sparklers at home — and Mill Woods Park on November 8 for the fireworks.
